items: the speech of Egypt — the language's own name
the great house — the word English took as pharaoh
good, beautiful, complete — the nefer of Nefertiti
may he live, be prosperous and healthy — written after a king's name
egyp1246.note: Hieroglyphs with Egyptological transliteration. Vowels are not written, so the readings are conventional rather than reconstructed pronunciation.

items: Whan that Aprille with his shoures soote
when April with its sweet showers — the opening of the Canterbury Tales
midd1317.note: Spelling was not standardised; these are common forms.

items: Carles li reis, nostre emperere magnes
Charles the king, our great emperor — the opening of the Chanson de Roland
oldf1239.note: Two-case Old French; forms vary by region and date.

latv1249.note: Latvian is living; ASJP simply never sampled it.

items: awakened one — the word used for Buddha
clas1254.note: Wylie transliteration beside the Tibetan script. The spelling froze in the seventh century, so written clusters are no longer pronounced.

impe1235.note: Given in square script, the form most Aramaic was later copied in.

items: Aryan — what its speakers called their own language
king; the title of the Kushan rulers
made — the word that opens most Bactrian inscriptions
king of kings — the Kushan imperial title on the Rabatak inscription
bact1239.note: Bactrian is the only Iranian language ever written in the Greek alphabet — a legacy of Alexander that outlasted Greek rule by seven hundred years. The letter þ (sho) was added for a sound Greek did not have.

items: the people, the community — cognate with German Deutsch and Irish tuath
the chief magistrate of an Oscan town
magistrate of the people — the highest office
land of calves — one proposed origin of the name Italy
household slave — Latin borrowed it as familia
let them go — the word that opens the Pompeii wall notices directing defenders to their posts
osca1245.note: Written in an alphabet of its own, derived from Etruscan and read right to left. That script is not reproduced here: the transliteration below is the scholarly convention, printed in every edition of the inscriptions, and the letterforms are the part that could not be set with confidence.

items: of Iguvium, the town — modern Gubbio
the priestly brotherhood whose rites the tables record
the people under arms — Latin populus
let him make, let him sacrifice — the commonest verb on the tables
umbr1253.note: Recorded almost entirely on the Iguvine Tables, seven bronze plates found at Gubbio in 1444 which set out the ritual duties of a priestly brotherhood — the fullest surviving account of any Italic religion outside Rome. Three tables are in the native Umbrian alphabet, four in Latin letters; the transliteration below is the convention used in every edition.

sogd1245.note: The trade language of the Silk Road, written in a script descended from Aramaic. Those letterforms are not reproduced here; the transliteration is the standard one. The best-known Sogdian texts are the Ancient Letters, a mailbag abandoned in a watchtower west of Dunhuang around 313 and never delivered.

items: Khotanese — the language's own name, from the name of the kingdom
khot1251.note: An Iranian language of the Silk Road oasis of Khotan, written in Brahmi and preserved almost entirely in Buddhist manuscripts recovered from the Taklamakan. The Brahmi letterforms are not reproduced here; the transliteration is the standard scholarly one.

items: the Silesian language — what its speakers call it
child — from German Beutel, and unlike anything in Polish
coal mine — the word a whole region's working life turned on
sile1253.note: Written in Latin letters with a Polish-derived orthography agreed in 2010, the ślabikŏrzowy szrajbōnek, which added ō and ŏ for vowels Polish does not have.

items: the language's own name — Roman, as in Eastern Roman
bread — the -ν that Modern Greek dropped is still there
I see — from ancient βλέπω, with a vowel Modern Greek lost
pont1253.note: Greek that left the rest of Greek early enough to keep sounds the standard lost — the infinitive survives, and so does the ancient ē where Modern Greek has i. Written in the Greek alphabet, and in Turkey by Muslim speakers in Latin letters.

items: a northerner, and the language — from ch'est ti, ch'est mi
dog — Picard keeps the k where French palatalised it to chien
cat — likewise, against French chat; English took its cat from the same Norman-Picard side
a downpour — the word Belgian French borrowed
pica1241.note: Written in Latin letters with several competing spellings, the Feller-Carton system being the most used. Its speakers in France call it chtimi, from the way northern French renders 'c'est toi, c'est moi'.

items: to do, to make — with the j where Castilian has h and Latin had f
extr1243.note: Astur-Leonese written in Latin letters, with almost no standard: its written tradition is essentially the poems of José María Gabriel y Galán at the turn of the twentieth century.

items: I — where Standard Hindi uses this for we
a greeting, used across religions in Fiji
fiji1242.note: Written in Devanagari and in Latin letters. Its vocabulary is Awadhi and Bhojpuri levelled together, with Fijian and English words that no Indian variety has.

items: hello — from guten Tag, worn down
the dimpled half-litre wine glass of the Palatinate
pala1330.note: Palatine German, written in Latin letters with no fixed standard. It is the ancestor of Pennsylvania German, which is why the two look alike on the page.
